utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. Whereas we were alerted to the 9.30 start tomorrow morning, we didn't know about the one this morning. For the record, we will sitting for today and the remainder of this week under Rule 15 bis; Judge Harhoff being absent. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. For the Prosecution, Tom Hannis and Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic, appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Aleksandar Aleksic for the Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And may we have the witness escorted back to the stand, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, good morning to you. As may have been explained, the reason for the late start today is for technical reasons. Before Mr. Hannis continues his cross-examination, I remind you you're still on your oath. Yes, please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to start with one of the documents we looked at on Friday and that I gave you a copy of to look at over the weekend. That's the -- that's 65 ter 20218. This is the minutes of the collegium in November 1993. And we saw before that you and Mr. Drljaca were present at that meeting. But I just had one question to ask you about, and it's at page 8 of the English in e-court. Pages 8 and 9. And in the B/C/S, it starts at page 7 and goes onto page 8 of the B/C/S. For you, Mr. Macar, I think it's the page numbered 5. It's Stojan Zupljanin speaking. Do you find that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And he is explaining his proposal on giving contracts to the non-Serb employees. And if you go onto the next page, there's a note that Mr. Kijac, Mr. Bjelosevic, Krsto Savic, and Milenko Karisik disagreed with Mr. Zupljanin's proposal. And that you -- my English has your last name spelled wrong, but in the B/C/S we see: "Goran Macar stressed that such people could not work for the forensic department during the war." Is that an accurate reflection of your position at the time, that you didn't think non-Serbs should work for the forensic department?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, before I begin with my reply to this question, I would like the OTP to present me the transcript of the session, if possible, as well as the rule-book on the job classification of the Ministry of the Interior that was in force at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I don't have either one of those documents, and I would ask that the witness try and answer the question as best he can, whether or not what's written reflects his position at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Macar. It's a fair question. If you -- to the extent that you're able to answer it, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The item of the agenda was the report on the activities aimed at assigning job duties to employees of the ministry and the manufacturing of official IDs to authorised officials. In order to better understand what assigning job duties means in 1993, let me explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Macar. I just want to know if it was your position in November 1993 that non-Serbs should not have jobs in the forensic department. Can you answer that yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was not my position that non-Serbian employees could not work in the forensic department, nor was that the position of Kijac, Bjelosevic, Savic or Karisik. That is why I cannot give a yes or no answer. Instead, I must explain what the discussion was about. These minutes --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, please --

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- are not certified and I --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, I have limited time. We had a late start today. I'm just asking you if what is said there is correct. And I gather from your answer, you're saying the way it's written down there is not correct. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't stated anything like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let's go onto another document then. We see Mr. Drljaca is still working for the MUP in 1993. I want to show you 65 ter 1470. This is tab 102 in the Prosecution's list. I'm sorry, this is just a short one-page document. I'll ask if you can make it out on the screen. It's dated the 15th of May, 1993, from the minister Ratko Adzic, apparently addressed to the executive committee of the Municipal Assembly in Prijedor. It says that Mr. Adzic is appointing Mr. Drljaca to their commission for investigating crimes of genocide. And it notes that Mr. Drljaca is head of the information office in the minister's cabinet. You were aware in 1993, weren't you, that Mr. Drljaca was in that position in the minister's cabinet?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. But, if I may add, Mr. Ratko Adzic was appointed minister. I don't know pursuant to whose nomination. And he may have been a good man in another position but --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Please, I haven't asked you to comment --

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I haven't asked you to comment on Mr. Adzic. Again, I have limited time. I'm sure you would like to be done with me as I would like to be done with you. So please try and focus on my questions and just answer my questions.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just half a sentence. It won't take much of your time, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Due to some activities of Mr. Adzic's, some senior officers of the ministry filed a request to the government to remove him. And I don't believe that he stayed in office long.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. In 1993, did you know a Colonel Bogojevic from the VRS. He was in the security administration for the VRS in General Mladic's Main Staff or General Staff. Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember meeting him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You knew Mile Matijevic from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to show you Exhibit P1767. And I can hand you a hard copy. Although this is a handwritten document and may not be easy for you to read. With the usher's assistance, and I will tell you this is in evidence as an excerpt from one of the diaries --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could we have the tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, it's tab 92 on the Prosecution's list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I've put a sticky tab on there to show you the part I want to ask you about specifically. It's an entry recorded as reflecting what Colonel Bogojevic is saying. He says that: "Four, five days ago, Simo Drljaca arrived. He was sent by the minister, and he came about the Tomasica mine." This is an entry from the 27th of May, 1993, by the way. And goes on to say. "... that mine near Prijedor where earlier they had buried about 5.000 Muslims. Drljaca came to leave this with us and they want to get rid of it by burning, grinding or some other way. There are all kinds of bodies, and they have involved Subotic in this. This team includes Drljaca. He was in charge even while this was being done. At the meeting were General Subotic, Arsic, Drljaca, me," Bogojevic, I guess, "and Mile Matijevic from the Banja Luka or BL SUP. I ask you for your position." And then an asterisk, "My position," and based on the testimony of General Milovanovic we take this to mean General Mladic, "they killed them so they should get rid of them?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, shouldn't we have this on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, we should, Your Honour. And I'm sorry, I didn't realise it was not up. It starts at page 4 and goes on to page 5 of the English. And in the B/C/S, in e-court it starts on page 4, and goes on page 5. I apologise, Your Honour, I wasn't looking at the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There, on the English, you see the first paragraph and once you've had a minute, perhaps we can go on to page 2. Mr. Macar, did you ever hear about these 5.000 bodies in the mine that's mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And we saw that on the 17th of May, apparently, Ratko Adzic was still the minister. This is reflecting something that would have happened about four or five days earlier than the 27th of May. So do you know if Mr. Adzic was still the minister on the 22nd or 23rd of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot specify the date he was removed, but it was done upon the initiative of some officials of the MUP because he was disrupting the organisational and functional system of the ministry. Because the man didn't know much about these things, nor about the functioning of public administration, the Ministry of the Interior included. I don't know the exact date when he was removed. I can't remember until I see ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know when Mr. Mico Stanisic became minister of the interior of the RS for the second time? Do you recall when that was?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me show you another one now. This is tab 66 of the Prosecution's list. 65 ter 20151. And, again, it's just a one-page document so I'll ask if you can look at the monitor. It's dated the 16th of May, 1994. It's from Simo Drljaca, as chief of the CJB.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, did I -- I said -- it's tab 66, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, CJB, what does that stand for?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Public security centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Is -- is that the same as the old CSB?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When did the terminology change from CSB to CJB; if you recall?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was done in the framework of the change of internal organisation. But I haven't seen a document showing the exact date, and I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And we see from this document that apparently Mr. Drljaca, in 1994, is the chief of the -- the public security centre in Prijedor. And the minister is Mr. Mico Stanisic; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: So we can see from the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this is from Mr. Drljaca to his SJBs informing him about appointments made by the minister which include Mr. Kovac, as acting head of public security; you, as chief of crime prevention, and number 6, Mile Matijevic, who we saw in General Mladic's diary entry as your deputy chief; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. The other one I want to ask you about is the Law on Administration, Law on State Administration. Did you have a chance to look at that? This is L0032 from the law library. I'm not sure what tab it was in the Prosecution's list. Oh, 113. And the reason I had asked you to look at that was to see if you could point to me an article or provision in that law that stands for the proposition that Crisis Staffs could not pass regulations or laws on subject matters that were already covered by some other law. Were you able to do that; and, if so, can you tell which provision that is?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll even amend what I said initially. We spoke about the powers of the executive bodies at municipal level, which means the executive committee and the Municipal Assembly and these powers were later assumed by the Crisis Staffs. I began to reply to your question by saying how things were regulated and who had which remit. And I mentioned the Law on Public Administration. Now I can add the constitution, the Law on Public Administration, the Law on Local Administration, the Law on Ministries that regulates the respective remits, down to municipal bodies. In order to learn what the powers of the municipal authorities were, you have to study these laws and regulations, and it so happened that when I was taking my intern's exam, way back in 1978, I had to learn the basics of the organisation of public administration, and that's where I got this information. In order to assist the Trial Chamber to understand this matter, I would like to remind you that the Ministry of the Interior of the RS, just like the former ministry of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was a centralised public administration body headed by the minister, and it has in place a system of subordination from the top of the ministry down to the public security station. That's a public administration body of the republic, which means that the public security station is not a municipal administration body to which the local executive committee and the local Assembly can give instructions or orders. By that very fact, the Crisis Staff that had taken over the powers of the executive committee of the municipality and the Municipal Assembly could not be in charge of the public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I know about public administration, which goes back to my internship, and I don't want to go on elaborating about the individual pieces of legislation. But this is among the basics that I had to learn when doing my -- when taking my exam at the end of my internship.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I -- I think -- I don't want to go over the discussion we had before about Article 27 of the Law on Internal Affairs. So let me move onto another topic. I want to talk to you about Exhibit 1D348. This is at tab 65. I think it's a Defence -- yes, it's a Defence document. So that will be in your binder from Mr. Zecevic, if you want to have a look at it. And that's your report -- or the report of the commission that you were on with Mr. Spasojevic, and Mr. Gajic, I think. It's dated the 31st of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Number 65? Tab 65. Do you recall how long or how many days your commission worked on putting together this report? It looks like the commission was set up by a decision dated the 20th of August. So ten days?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, thereabouts, since it was typed on the 31st.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, prior to August 20th, had you been -- had you been working directly for Mr. Kljajic? Were you -- were you in Bijeljina at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 20th? Well, yes, I was in Bijeljina in August. On those days, I may have gone to Trebinje or Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you -- did you or anyone on the commission interview Mr. Kljajic in connection with this report?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The report was commissioned as a consequence of the information received that Mr. Dragan Andan had taken a poker machine, I believe, from the depository of the public security station of Bijeljina for some operative needs. I don't know if that information had been received from citizens or another way; but, at any rate, the ministry was aware of that. And that was the first thing that was checked. It was established that Mr. Andan had Mr. Cedo Kljajic's approval to take that machine. I don't doubt his honest intentions, and I don't doubt that he did so for official purposes, but it was established that it wasn't done in accordance with the procedure that was in place for something like that too. After the end -- and I believe that even disciplinary proceedings were initiated against Mr. Andan and that he was relieved from his duty because of that procedural fault. And since we had the information that Mr. Kljajic had approved his act, the minister ordered that the entire depository be inspected, and that's why this commission was set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. This report, it's three pages long. I think I see Mr. Andan's name mentioned three times; whereas, the bulk of the remaining checks and findings relate to Mr. Kljajic, who is mentioned eight or nine times. Let me ask you: When and where was the last time you saw Mr. Kljajic in 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember whether it was in late October or early November.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall how you first realised or discovered or learned that he was, indeed, gone from the MUP?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an agreement with the minister first, and then one gained an insight into the status of the deposits. This was then forwarded for further operative processing and checks which, among other things, envisaged a number of interviews with a number of persons, additional checks regarding the deposit, and I think this was something that was done by the public security station holding the actual deposit. The procedure took at least a month or two because some persons were away on the front line, or for other reasons. I believe it was sometime in late October or early November that this particular issue was analysed. It was round about this time that I noticed that Mr. Kljajic had been away for quite a long time, that he actually wasn't there at all. I received information suggesting that he left for the Republic of Serbia, and I have not seen him since, quite literally.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I know from collegium meetings that Mr. Kljajic is listed as attending the collegium on the 3rd of October and the one on the 5th of November, 1992. So, as far as these findings of your commission relate to Mr. Kljajic, was any disciplinary action initiated or taken against him, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not right away, I don't think. The assessment was that checks should be conducted in relation to each and every item from the report that required further interviews or checks. I think it was up to the public security station to do that. The security centre had not been set up by this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The findings as described in your report, if they turned out to be true, would they amount to something that could be prosecuted as a violation of the Criminal Code?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This depended on the checks that were conducted. That's why the record was drawn up, saying that further checks should be conducted, in order to establish whether there were any elements of crime involved or not. Nevertheless, once the operative procedure was over, we were no longer able to get in touch with Mr. Kljajic. Now, as I said, I can't remember whether all of this was happening in late October or early November, which leaves me unable to speculate as to the date. We then went to Pale and then back to Bijeljina and we were preparing our move. So I can't remember exactly but it to had be to either late October or early November. He had been gone for as long by this time. Perhaps you're interested in hearing my own position based on my conversations with the minister. Had we had all the operative material available to us at the time, we certainly would have taken certain detention measures against Mr. Kljajic. If I'd had the kind of operative material available to me, indicating the commission of any crime and given his position, steps like that would have been taken, I can say that much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. In anything you heard from the minister or anybody else in the collegium, did you find out whether Mr. Kljajic had given any kind of notice to the MUP or to the minister that he was leaving? Or did he just go, in essence, abandon his post and leave? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if he gave any kind of notice. I know that most of his colleagues didn't know where he was or what he was doing. The one thing I do know for sure is he didn't tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think you said last week that you heard he gone to Serbia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information available to me at the time indicated that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And am I correct in understanding that if he had left the MUP and remained in the Republika Srpska, he would be subject to being sent to the army, because the war was on; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kljajic did have a war assignment, and it was actually a high-ranking one within the Ministry of the Interior. Based on that retroactive procedure, that need not have been the case. He could have used his private contacts to get a position in some lower-ranking units. I can't speculate any further, but my information at the time certainly suggested he was somewhere in the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your answer, you said you could have used his private contacts to get a position in some lower-ranking unit. You mean within the RS MUP?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I mean in the RS -- in the VRS. There was a shortage of men in all of the units. Any senior officer would have been eager to get another man capable of carrying a rifle. But this all amounts to mere speculation. It certainly is a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you or anyone in the RS MUP, as far as you know, send an attempt to locate Mr. Kljajic to the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember whether that was done at the time. The case was being handled by the public security station. I know that he was unavailable for an interview. As the acting coordinator in that case, I was busy elsewhere. Even this information wasn't verified information at the time, suggesting that he was somewhere in the -- the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And do you know if -- for a fact that he's alive and well today and living abroad?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You -- you just don't know one way or another; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, on the other hand, as far as Mr. Andan was concerned, there wasn't much delay in doing something about him; right? Did you know that he was disciplined very shortly after this report was issued?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Mr. Dragan Andan's case, this was something that was unrelated to this report. We obtained information back in August that Mr. Andan was using a poker machine in some facility or other, or that he had requisitioned a poker machine from the depot. And that's why the Andan case was opened and checks were being made; at least as far as I can remember. Mr. Andan's explanation for all that was that this item was being used for operative purposes. I think there was a note that was written up and that he was actually allowed to use the machine by Mr. Kljajic. Nevertheless, in order to use an item or an object like that for operative purposes, one must process this in a procedurally correct way, showing why a case was being opened and to collect just what information specifically. Once that was done, approval would have been sought to use a thing like a poker machine, for example, an item like that, perhaps some funds, and so on and so forth. Unfortunately, the procedure was not observed. There is one thing you could notice about back in 1992. The minister himself issued orders on the need to observe discipline, checks, control. It was established beyond a shadow of a doubt that procedures had not been followed. Therefore, one was not allowed to use this poker machine for operative purposes, and that's why disciplinary proceedings were set in motion. After that, I'm not sure whether the minister was actually in possession of any other information. One thing that I do know is that he was now issuing an order to check the depot in Bijeljina. In order to check the depot, you first gather certain types of information, data, and so on and so forth, whereupon you take operative steps to establish the actual facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you P1269, which is tab 87. And with the usher's help, I'll hand you a hard copy. This is a record of the collegium meeting held on the 9th of September, 1992, at the Kosuta facility on Mount Jahorina. You'll see on the first page the listing of those attending, and you're listed as being present, as well as Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Kljajic, among others. I'd like you to go to page -- well, I've tabbed the page for you. It's page 7 -- or 6 in English. I think it's the next -- I'm sorry. If you could go back one page. There's a list of persons against whom disciplinary measures --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's page 3 in the Serbian text, the last paragraph. It starts and it --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- goes on to page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You see the bottom of page 3, number one is Mr. Andan. "Dragan Andan temporarily suspended for illegal use of poker machine discovered by the working group which has been appointed by the minister." Right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So, is the minister able to suspend employees without a disciplinary proceeding having been conducted? Can he just do it immediately, or do the rules require some kind of procedure to take place first?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to answer that question, I would need to jog my memory about the rules on disciplinary proceedings. At the HQ, I didn't have the disciplinary proceedings, and for that reason, I can't remember specifically what the rules envisaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I don't know the answer myself. That's why I asked you -- Let me show you, then, Exhibit P2349, which is tab 98 of the Prosecution binder. And I'm sorry, Mr. Kljajic [sic], that's not in your binder. I can give you a hard copy of this one as well. And actually, I'll give you P2348 as well, which is tab 99. Because these two documents are closely connected. The first one -- they're both dated the 11th of September, 1992. If you'll look at the one that has number 09-2511 at the top. My English translation translated as a request to initiate proceedings to establish disciplinary responsibility against Dragan Andan. You find that one?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the statements of reasons makes reference to Andan requisitioning a gambling machine from the Bijeljina SJB depot. And the evidence is: "Dragan Andan confessed to me in the presence of Dusko Malovic and Sinisa Karan." While we're there, you knew Dusko Malovic, right? He was from Sokolac. You know him in 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's the man, yes. Sinisa Karan, yes, I know him. There's Dusko Malovic, the one from Sokolac, or a different Dusko Malovic, I really don't know. I do know Dusko Malovic from Sokolac. I met him back in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. The one that you knew in 1992, was he the head of a special police platoon?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was commander of a unit from the public security centre in Sarajevo. I'm not sure what level the unit was. Was it a platoon, a company? Not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And his unit, we've been told, was referred to sometimes as Mico Stanisic's Men. Did you ever hear that term used for them?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the men working there may possibly have called them that. I know that some men from the administration under me were referred to as Macar's Men. I can't say that I ever witnessed that myself, anyone calling them Stanisic's Men. But it certainly would have been possible to apply that moniker to a number of persons working for the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And their unit, as I understand, was in Bijeljina in September of 1992; did you know that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I do know is that the unit was part of the special police detachment, specifically the component under the command of Mr. Davidovic, in the month of August. I don't know exactly whether they remained in Bijeljina for this long. I was busy elsewhere, so there was no way I could know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this unit, we're told, wore some rather unique camouflage uniform. Rather than green or blue, it was primarily grey, white, and black. You recall their unusual camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many units had different uniforms, blue, just plain overalls, or combat uniforms. What would their peculiarity be as compared to other units at the time, I don't know. People got whatever they could at the time in terms of uniform. We still didn't have the sort of uniformity, in terms of uniform that was required. There were many wearing combat uniforms. Some were even wearing police uniforms. All kinds of different uniforms in one word.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I calculate it's been about an hour. Is this an appropriate time for the first break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, it was near 9.30 that we started, so I intended to run until 10.30 and take the break then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll continue on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Sinisa Karan, what was his job and where was he working in September 1992? Was he stationed at Bijeljina? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sinisa Karan was dispatched to Bijeljina a lot earlier than that. Perhaps even as far back as Mr. Vukovic and Mr. Andan. What was his position in Bijeljina, though, was he working with the public security station, I can't remember. I do know that he was transferred to the crime police administration later on, late that year or thereabouts, but you should really check his file to see the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And the second document is the one that is numbered 09-2512. 09 is a reference to which administration in the RS MUP? Is it legal affairs?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes. And personnel too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And the second one is the decision. And it's the decision based on the request we saw in the other document, which is referenced here by number. So the request is made by Mr. Stanisic on the 11th. And the decision temporarily suspending Dragan Andan is made on the 11th of September by Mr. Stanisic. But this is two days after the collegium meeting on the 9th, where it said that he was already temporarily suspended. Do you have any explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as this decision is concerned, the question should probably be addressed to someone from legal and personnel affairs. I don't know under what conditions this decision was made. It's not for me to say because that wasn't my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. On -- on the 11th of July, you were talking about the document that purported to authorise Mr. Kovac to sign for the minister during his absence. I think that was dated the 21st of October, 1992. But Mr. Stanisic was still -- still on the job and working as the minister in November and December of 1992, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which document are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's the one that was not signed but you told us you'd seen the original. It's just a very short document saying, "I hereby authorise Tomo Kovac to sign for me." Do you remember that one? I can find it, if you need to see it, but ...

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the document, not the date of the document, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's tab 77 in our binder, if --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's tab 77 in your binder, Mr. Macar, if you want to have a look. But my question was: Mr. Stanisic was still working and holding his position as minister in November and December of 1992; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he remained there until his replacement. I can't say exactly to what extent he was able to exercise his function for all the reasons that I've mentioned. I know that most of the communication at the time was with Mr. Kovac. With the exception of the things that I know and told you about, I can't address anything else that went on at the higher levels. There was pressure being exerted on the ministry, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall him presiding at the collegium meeting in Bijeljina on the 5th of November, 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I would need to see the actual minutes. There were just so many meetings. It's difficult to distinguish the dates. If you could please show me the minutes --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I'm certain that I could remember when the meeting was held and what it was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The last one then before the break, we'll show the witness Exhibit P1270, tab 54 of the Prosecution list. I think it's tab 86, actually, in your Defence binder. 86. You see Mr. Stanisic presiding over that meeting, where you're listed as an attendee?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would this be an appropriate point, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. We return in 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, a general question about procedure in relation to the collegium meetings. We see that the minutes are typed up. Are these then circulated to you and the other people who attended the meeting afterward? Was it standard practice for you to get a copy of the record of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody was supposed to get a copy, but we didn't always get one. At the meeting, everybody takes notes of the conclusions and of their respective tasks for the coming period. That is why we didn't really insist on receiving a copy. But there were cases when the minutes were distributed to everybody, to all or maybe not each and every one. But there certainly were cases where the minutes were not distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the event that you got a copy of the minutes and saw that something was incorrect, was not reported the way you said it or meant it, you would have an opportunity to have that changed; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even when the minutes were distributed to a senior officer - me, for instance - I didn't have to be in my office all the time, because I was out in the field a lot. I didn't really do that. And you see how these minutes were taken. When I speak fast here, sometimes the interpreters don't catch everything. It is much the same at a meeting. Sometimes only a sentence or half a sentence is put down and mentioned in the minutes, although the original presentation was much longer. And if you read the minutes, you sometimes wonder what did the people do there for so many hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. That -- that causes me to want to go back to the first one I showed you this morning, 65 ter 20218, tab 120, for two more questions. This is that collegium from November 1993. I think you still have a hard copy. That is the one that you took over the weekend, one of the two documents. Do you have it there? There it is, I think, yeah. And if you could go to the page where I'd asked you about whether that reflected what you said about people working in the forensic department. I know your answer about that. But, Mr. Kijac, Mr. Bjelosevic, Mr. Savic, and Mr. Karisik are simply reported as having said they disagreed with Mr. Zupljanin's proposal. That's correct, isn't it? They just disagreed with what Mr. Zupljanin proposed about giving contracts to non-Serb employees.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You didn't let me answer why they disagreed. It wasn't only Mr. Zupljanin's proposal --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because those employees worked at the CJB before the collegium and after collegium.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I must say two or three sentences --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And I'm sorry also. This is the second time, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- the witness is trying to give the answer. Mr. Hannis is asking him then he stops him in the middle of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I didn't ask him --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is the four -- this is the second time. But the question -- he needs to explain on what they didn't agree with Mr. Zupljanin's proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is the gist of the question, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The precise question was did they disagree. I didn't ask why they disagreed. I'm just asking if this is accurately reported that they disagreed with his proposal. I'm not asking why. Mr. Zecevic can ask about that during his time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But, with all due respect, Your Honours, at the beginning of today's session, the first session, the very same question was asked and the witness said: No, that is -- I'm sorry. No, the recording here is wrong. They did not disagree. They did not. And now Mr. Hannis is asking again and the witness wants to explain, and again Mr. Hannis is blocking him. That's why I'm objecting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: His answer just now, at page 23, line 23, was, Let me tell you why they disagreed. I infer from that he is now saying, Yes, they did disagree. Let me tell you why. All I'm asking is, is that correct, correctly recorded, if they disagreed. And he has said yes. If he wants to answer why, he can do that on re-direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you could go back to the page where it has Mr. Zupljanin explaining his proposal, if would you read that and tell me, do you remember is that an accurate reflection of what he said at the time? Or do you remember? It was almost 18 years ago.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to me that the most concise summary of what Mr. Zupljanin said is reflected here. But his presentation certainly contained much more detail, and if you were in a position to read that, you would be better put to understand the whole minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we do object. This document has no relevance for the -- for this case whatsoever. It's a November 1993 collegium. If this is a document that -- that -- that is supposed to -- to go to the credibility of the witness, then -- then the witness should be given the opportunity to answer. If it's -- if it's anything else, we do object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, without going down the road of separating credibility from other purposes, and by now counsel would have had the benefit of the Chamber's views on that distinction, the -- isn't there a problem in your tendering this document for the reason that -- and we come back to the -- well, as Mr. Zecevic has just said, that the -- apart from the fact that it's dealing with the collegium meeting in 1993, if you're using it for other purposes, then you have placed yourself into the position of having -- not only in fairness to the witness but in order for the comprehension of the Chamber of having the witness explain the answers which you had indicated earlier would be best left for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I could ask that the witness take his headphones off. Your Honours, as with most documents, I'm offering it for more than one purpose. One of the purposes this document is being offered for to show that Mr. Drljaca, in spite of good cause for him to be removed and in spite of claims by some witnesses that he was removed, indeed he wasn't removed in the sense of being kicked out of the MUP. He is in a higher position than he was as chief of the SJB in Prijedor. He is at the cabinet level in the ministry. So that's one purpose for this document. With regard to Mr. Zupljanin, it's been his position that he -- the Defence position that he no bias against non-Serbs and here is a reflection where he is saying, We should hire non-Serbs. That is consistent with the Defence, but from the Prosecution point of view, the rest of the answer suggests that, really, the reason that he is in favour of hiring non-Serbs is because of the public perception. He talks about the interests of journalists and media personnel in the fact that Banja Luka has hired non-Serbs. And that's part of the reason the Prosecution wants to answer, yes, there is some evidence that he appeared not opposed because he had non-Serbs working for him. But we say, in reply to that, yes, but that was for appearances' sake. So that's another reason that I would tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I hear all of that, Mr. Hannis, but I come back to the question as to the -- in order for this to be added as an exhibit, isn't the context necessary, hence the matters which the witness wished to expand upon, and which at that point, ex facie, appeared to be irrelevant for the limited purposes of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I think if I'm going to insist that his claim now that it's -- inaccurately reflects what he says goes to credibility, I suppose, yeah, he should be entitled to explain why it doesn't reflect what he said. But I'm more interested in tendering it for those other reasons than for his credibility. My arguments about his credibility are going to rely more on other documents and other answers than this one about something in November 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Your Honours, the reasons which Mr. Hannis just stated have nothing to do -- are irrelevant for this case, entirely irrelevant. First of all, Mr. Drljaca was appointed as -- as the aide of the minister during the time when Mr. Mico Stanisic was not a minister. Therefore, his position in the MUP is totally irrelevant in respect to our clients and the subject matter of this case because it is limited until 1992, the whole 1992. As for Stojan Zupljanin, the state of mind of the -- of the accused in the end of 1993, as opposed to 1992, I don't see how that can be even more -- even relevant at all. Therefore we strongly object, and there has been a number of occasions when the Office of the Prosecutor was using the same, precisely the same reasons when we offered the documents which were even more specifically targeting events in 1992, where they were saying that it is irrelevant because it's from 1993. This particular document has no connection with the situation in 1992 whatsoever, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Really, Your Honour, I expected Mr. Aleksic to speak for Mr. Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully agree with what my learned friend Mr. Zecevic has said. I have nothing to add. As for the document itself, it is stated that Mr. Zupljanin submitted his speech in writing which the witness has also mentioned. If we don't have that either, then that's one more reason to consider the document irrelevant, in addition to what Mr. Zecevic has said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, don't we have the evidence about Mr. Simo Drljaca in the -- in the cabinet in previous documents that you tendered today or --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Friday, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- last Friday -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So this is just repetitive in that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think the previous document I had was when Mr. Adzic was the minister, and in November of 1993, it was someone else other than Mr. Adzic, and before Mr. Stanisic returned for his second term. So I guess I'm trying to show a continuous stream of Mr. Drljaca being employed in the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In the Chamber's view, this document doesn't assist and it would not be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, let me go now to some documents dealing with the issue of prisoners and detained persons. I'd like to show you P427.18. This is tab 121 in the Prosecution's list. And I think it will assist you if we can give you a hard copy. While you're waiting for the hard copy, I'll tell you it's a -- it's the minutes of a Presidency session dated the 6th of August, 1992. And to put it in chronology, this is just the time that some of the international media about persons detained in Manjaca and Omarska and Keraterm is being broadcast in the greater public. I want to specifically ask you about something that's on your page 2, and page 2 of the English. There's a reference to the work of the Commission for Investigating War Crimes Committed Against the Serbian People in the Serbian Republic of BH and the former Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Did you know about the existence of this commission in the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we looking at the same document?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I hope so. Page 2. Yes, page 2, the back of that page. It's a two-sided document. The one in your right hand. Did you know of the existence of that commission?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned of its existence in late 1992. I had many problems because of the way they worked, or, to be more precise, because they didn't pass on information. In 1993 or 1994, I even wanted to search the premises and even the private home of a man who was a commission member. Toward the end of 1992, I held the opinion that the commission was to collect documents to be analysed and so on. I didn't see it as a commission that would assume some powers of the MUP or military security organs. And the worst thing is that from early 1993, which you were able to see because you had access to the archives of crime enforcement, we contacted that commission at least twice a year with very specific requests. According to the information I had, the commission was to be part of some sort of documentation centre for war crimes and not a commission that would actually investigate war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you --

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ministry, I believe it was in 1994, had some problems because of our efforts to place the problem of war crimes under the jurisdiction of the ministry of the -- of justice and military judiciary bodies. But we didn't have any documents, so that in 1994, we wanted to conduct a search if for no other reason than for the reasons of concealment of documents about crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Against Serbs; correct? That's what this commission was for.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a commission for documenting war crimes, as far as I know. Whether they were tasked to collect evidence about crimes against one side or another side is -- is something I don't know. But we did get documents from the army and lower-ranking units, from combat areas, then from citizens who had escaped from the territory controlled by the opponent. But then there was some information that was not accessible to the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Macar, you see the name in the document. It's a Commission for Investigating War Crimes Committed Against the Serbian People. That's the name of the committee. Doesn't that reflect what its job is? Or, if you don't know, say so.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen this document before. And it was my idea --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Please --

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that the task --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Macar.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- of the commission was to set up a documentation centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Please try and focus on my specific question and answer that, if you can. Let me ask you this: Do you know who any of the members of the commission were in 1992; and, if so, what was their job in real life, apart from being on the commission?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that one of the members I had communication with as of 1993, I think, was Mr. Toholj. I believe that he was minister of information for a while. Let me try and remember. Trbojevic, I think, or somebody. It's based on information from the field that I got information about this commission. I got it from crime police operatives who informed the administration that at Pale there was a commission for documenting war crimes which is contacted by citizens, that is, refugees, from the territories controlled by the enemy, and the commission was also getting documents from some military units which they had obtained during combat and seizing enemy documents. And there were attempts to establish communication to see what their activity consisted in and whether we could get access to materials that were security relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Anybody from the MUP a member of the commission in 1992? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Commission for Documenting War Crimes, as I remember from early 1991 ... but, anyway, toward the end of 1992, I received information about that commission. There may have been MUP members on the commission when it was established. But in 1993, I don't think so because it was a body that was dealing with matters that were from the jurisdiction of other institutions. If we're talking about the same thing. Because it's not an ad hoc commission. It was a commission that was meant to be active for a longer time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One clarification. Your answer is recorded: "In 1993, I don't think there were MUP members." Did you mean 1992 or what?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said already that I learned about the existence of the commission in late 1992 or in early 1993. And according to the information that I had received, I took them to be a commission documenting war crimes rather than investigating.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The question was -- you partially answered and said: "There may have been MUP members on the commission when it was established. But in 1993, I don't think ..." So the question is: Were there MUP members on the commission in 1992, if you know?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I see --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The document you have, if you could continue on from where we left off, it's talking about the treatment of prisoners of war detained in prisons in Serbian territory being discussed. And if you could go on to the third page, there's a conclusion that says: "The MUP -- the Ministry of the Interior ... will be ordered to examine through its municipal branches the behaviour of all civilian authorities and individuals guarding prisoners of war. The information will be passed to the MUP which will pass it to the Presidency ..." Were you aware that this task was ordered for the Ministry of the Interior and was it being carried out after the 6th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously I'm not the right person to answer this question because, as you know, in August, I worked in Bijeljina on a specific task as operative coordinator. And I see that this document is dated 6th August. I cannot comment on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that answer. But it appears to be an ongoing task and so I take it after August 6th, you didn't see any -- anything to indicate whether this was something that was being done in the MUP at the level of the SJBs? For example, in the course of the instructive tours, nothing was reported back to you from your inspectors about that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you know, and as I have already said, I know about it from a later period, but I don't know any details that commissions were established and that there was information flow toward the ministry. I know from visits in late 1992 that, at a certain time, in Samac, there was a prison, or camp, or a collection centre, I don't know, but I don't know whether it was in existence during our visit. Probably not. But at an earlier time, the police were engaged in that facility. That was in late 1992, when we were visiting the Doboj centre and the Samac station.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at a report from another SJB that talks a little bit about detained persons and how that was handled in Prijedor. This is Exhibit P684. It's tab 115. And I'll ask the usher to give you a hard copy of this one. Mr. Macar, this is from Simo Drljaca, and it appears to be the report for the third quarter of 1992 on the activities of Prijedor SJB. Did you see this document before? Is this the first time you've seen it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a document sent to the Security Services Centre of Banja Luka. I don't think I've ever seen the document in this format before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. In terms of these kinds of quarterly and semi-annual and annual reports from SJBs, is that something that you or your inspectors would have occasion to see in connection with your instructive tours or on occasion of formulating your own end-of-the-year report at headquarters level. Is this something that you would see?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that following one of your previous questions I established that in 1992 the information flow from the public security stations to the centre and to the ministry HQ, for objective reasons, was not possible, at least not the kind of quality that would allowed the ministry to know what was really going on further afield. And that is why there followed orders from the minister, midway through that year and in some documents later on, for periodic reports to be produced. When visiting or touring police stations on the ground, and the visit to Prijedor happened at a very late stage, people from the crime police wanted information, first and foremost, technical information on the resources and so on and so forth. They would visit all the departments and units and wanted to know about the crime situation in each of these areas. When we did this on our own, we didn't deal with the active or reserve police issues but only our own speciality, crime-related issues. As I said, those were the first visits, and one attempted to take in the general situation in the group, department or unit itself, including the overall situation regarding crime in a certain municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, if we could go to page 5 of the English, and I'm not sure what page it is in the B/C/S since I've given away my hard copy. Mr. Macar, there's a reference to the third quarter of 1992, especially months of July and August, being characterised by the processing and investigation of Muslim and Croatian extremists in Keraterm and Omarska reception centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Second paragraph on page 3 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you find that? Are you with me?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 3, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it says that: "Operational and investigative activities determined those persons interesting for security reasons who directly or indirectly participated in the armed rebellion in the Prijedor municipality, and all operatives participated in the processing of these persons." I take this to mean that the operatives from Prijedor SJB helped with that work at Keraterm and Omarska. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my inference too. I don't know whether that is correct, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Fair enough. If we could go to page 8 of the English. I think it's the last page for you, Mr. Macar. Just one question --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry -- I'm terribly sorry. Again, we have a -- I believe we have a problem with the interpretation. On the previous page, if we can return back. Perhaps the witness can read, because I don't think the whole sentence is missing [sic] in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you be a little more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The -- the page 3, the part which you read. Oh, it's okay, I'm sorry. I'm terribly sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Macar, are you on the last page? Yeah, you see a highlighted paragraph. This is dealing with communications from Prijedor. You see it says it's sent 696 dispatches, 678 which were unsealed and 18 were in code. Do you see that one? Yes. Now, above that, it says that they received and there's a number that can't be read, I guess, from the B/C/S copy. "... of which 234 were unsealed and 19 were coded." Would you agree with me that probably that illegible number should be 253 because that is the total of coded and uncoded documents? 19 plus 234 equals 253. Makes sense, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'm going to ask you about another topic now. In 1992, did you ever hear about the six strategic goals of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: After 1992, did you ever hear about the six strategic goals that were first pronounced at an Assembly session on the 12th of May, 1992? Did you never hear about that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me show you Exhibit P -- let me show you Exhibit P187. And this was tab 82 in the Prosecution's list. It will be up on the screen in a minute. It's just a one-page document. You see this is the decision. And this -- the objectives are a border separation between the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the other two national communities. A corridor between Semberija and Krajina. A corridor in the valley of the Drina so as to eliminate any border between the RS and the Republic of Serbia. Another border on the Una and Neretva rivers. Division of Sarajevo into Serbian and Muslim parts. And an exit for the RS to the sea. You never heard of these six strategic objectives. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never heard of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in conjunction with Crisis Staffs, did you ever hear of a document called the Variant A and Variant B instructions issued by the SDS in December of 1991? Did you never hear of that document?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I told you before, I was not a member of the SDS. I wasn't even close to the inner circle of the SDS leaders. I didn't know about their activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that. But you've given us a lot of evidence and testimony about Crisis Staffs, so I thought you may have heard of that document. Let me show you --

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me show you 65 ter -- it's tab 94. It's a map. It's 65 ter 20050. I can hand you a copy. I'll tell you this is from -- from the Defence expert's report, and this is a colour version of the map that was attached to one of his documents in his expert report. If the usher could assist me, I'll hand you this. It's a map of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it's colour coded. This was being used in conjunction with the discussions that were going on in late 1991 and early 1992 before the conflict broke out in April. Now I think you've told us it was your understanding that this new RS MUP was being created because of the agreement of the three parties. But you'll see that under the plan, a number of municipalities that were foreseen as Muslim areas were, indeed, taken over by the Serbs and Serb SJBs were established. For example, in Foca, Visegrad, Rogatica, Vlasenica, Bratunac, Zvornik, Brcko. So, in effect, isn't it true there wasn't agreement and the Bosnian Serbs had already decided which territories they wanted and that was further reflected in the strategic objectives we saw in that May 12th, 1992, document?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The six strategic objectives were part of the war operations. Therefore, I wasn't familiar with that. Nor, indeed, could I tell you anything now about the ethnic makeup back in 1992, 1991, or, indeed, 1990. I had an opportunity to share some information here, but I never saw the ethnic makeup represented like that. I couldn't tell you about the exact figures in any of the municipalities. Therefore, I'm hardly the right kind of person to talk to about that. The issue or, indeed, the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Isn't it true that -- that the civilian authorities and the Crisis Staffs, for example, and the police and the army were working together, sometimes better, sometimes not so well, but were working together to achieve those strategic objectives?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't address that. I can't say whether the strategic objectives were something that the municipal bodies were dealing with, or, indeed, the Ministry of the Interior, and, if so, to what extent. Had this been the case with the ministry, I think I would have bound to notice, to some extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Let me show you another document. This is it 65 ter 1640. I believe it is tab 43.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Tab 43.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And with the usher's help, I can give you a hard copy. It's dated the 12th of September, 1992. I don't know if you're able to read the last page of my copy. But I can tell you it comes from Commander Stanislav Galic from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. You know who he was; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of him, but I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. After the war, you've heard about who he was; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: On the first page, item number 3, he is talking about things that need to be done. And it says: "Ensure absolute agreement and unity with the civilian authorities and MUP forces at all levels. Eliminate the creation of any paramilitary units or para political, and eliminate any squabbles because we have the same goals." That's true, isn't it, what General Galic, or Colonel Galic at the time, is saying?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the specific item you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's number 3 on my list. Did you find it? "Ensure absolute agreement and unity with the civilian authorities and MUP forces at all levels. Eliminate ... paramilitary units ... eliminate any squabbles because we have the same goals." Do you disagree?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the question is?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct isn't it? That the police and the civilian authorities and the VRS had the same goals in September 1992.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If by objectives you mean the preservation of Republika Srpska and the establishment of appropriate authorities in Republika Srpska, to guarantee the safety of all citizens there, in that case the answer is yes. The objective of the army was to preserve the territory of Republika Srpska. The civilian authorities were to do their own jobs, including logistics for the army. The police were to do their work. The common objective was to preserve Republika Srpska and to make sure that it was functioning properly, as well as to ensure the safety of all its citizens and the survival of its economy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But as we saw on the 12th of May, the first strategic objective was a border separating from the other two ethnic parties; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would just remind Mr. Hannis to read the whole strategic objective if he is putting that to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Number 1 was border separation of the state from the other two national communities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The witness has indicated that we would take a break now --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Ah, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- and we're near the time for -- that we rise. So will --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the witness is coming in, I just wanted to inquire what time should I take the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I was seeing whether we could do with anything with this odd half-hour we would have at the end of the day if we sit according to the schedule we're having now. But I think it would be simpler to just continue the hour pattern and then the 15-minute break, and the half-hour that we lost this morning is simply irrecoverable. That's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mm-hm. So I was thinking I would take a break at 12.45 or 1.00 or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, between 12.45 and 1.00, depending on the witness's disposition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Tab 94 of your binder, you showed the witness the Cutileiro map. You remember?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You didn't tender that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is there a problem why it shouldn't be tendered? Is it a special number or something --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think the difference -- as I recall, that's a map that we took from one of the annexes to Mr. Bajagic's expert report and we had put in colour because I think what we had from him was a black and white version. And I don't remember if his map had the names of all the municipalities. I think that is how this map is different. But in terms what was showing what was Serb, Muslim and Croat, it's the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And where does this map come from, then? Is it something OTP put together?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah. We have colourised it and put in the names of the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Then perhaps you will object, Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: By all means, I would, Your Honours, because I don't know what was the basis for -- for -- for this colouration and adding and what is the original map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Yeah. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will get back to that, Your Honour, because I think that the showing of the territories was reflected on the black and white by various shades of grey and it was just putting in the names of the municipality, and I'll talk to Mr. Zecevic about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, you mentioned a conflict that existed between Mico Stanisic and the MUP on the one hand and Mrs. Plavsic, among others, on the other side. And this conflict was rooted, in part, over the fact that Mrs. Plavsic had early in the conflict invited outsiders to come and assist the Bosnian Serbs in the conflict, and a number of those people that she invited later turned out to be problems for the Republika Srpska, some of those volunteers. Is that a fair statement so far?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could say that that is one of the reasons. But the best part of the reason is a certain amount of misinformation in the work of the ministry, regrettably, also spread by Mr. Djeric and some others about Ms. Plavsic, or, rather, being forwarded in the direction of Ms. Plavsic, based on which she created an opinion concerning the minister and the work of the ministry. I know that in 1993, 1994, and 1995 there were continuing attacks on the ministry at meetings. Unfortunately, she never visited the ministry in order to familiarise herself with the MO of the Ministry of the Interior and any problems that we encountered in our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe the witness -- yeah. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to show you Exhibit P591. It's Prosecution tab 96. And if you could just look at the screen at the first page, it's up, I will tell that you is a report from the VRS, in particular from then-Colonel Tolimir and it's a report on paramilitary formations in the territory. Did you ever see this before?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'd appreciate a copy, in case you have a spare one for me. It's difficult for me to read this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I see Mr. Zecevic has one. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The usher will hand it to you in a second? Among those listed are Arkan's Men and Seselj's Men, Captain Dragan's Commandos, Carli's Men, and White Eagles. You're not saying, are you, that all of these groups were ones that came because of Mrs. Plavsic, are you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You were aware that these groups, like Arkan's Men and Seselj's Men, and White Eagles were operating in the territory in 1992 and in some cases committing crimes. They weren't merely defending the Serbian people in the RS and fighting in combat but they were also committing crimes; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the number and types of paramilitary formations active throughout the territory of Republika Srpska, I can't really say how many exactly there were. Some came as volunteers to the VRS. As far as some of them are concerned, we received information that they tore themselves away from their rightful commands in Foca and some other parts of the Krajina. It's very difficult for me to say which of these were brought in by Ms. Plavsic herself. The one thing I do remember is that there was one of these meetings at Pale attended by Ms. Plavsic herself. At this meeting she said she herself made an effort to get some volunteers in, but she didn't say which exactly; was it the Wolves, was it the Spare Ribs or whoever, she didn't say. I didn't hear of any of these at the time. I heard about some of them later. But one thing that I can say is that I didn't see this specific document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But my question was: You were aware that these groups, like Arkan's and Seselj's and White Eagles, not only were participating in combat, were also committing crimes in the RS. You knew about that, didn't you? Didn't hear about Seselj's Men committing crimes? Or Arkan's Men? Or White Eagles? You were the chief of the crime police in the RS MUP. You must have heard that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military formations were just that for me, military formations. As to their individual components, that's not something that I knew about it. The one thing I did hear, which was also one of the reasons that we started arresting people from those units, was the Yellow Wasps. All of that was under the jurisdiction of the military security people and the military police, so they did their job. Whenever our stations came by information, they would have by default informed our own security officers under who had jurisdiction they worked. I heard about the crimes committed by the Yellow Wasps specifically. But this was a job that was done by the security people of the army and the military prosecutor. I received no feedback as to whether they were successful in shedding any light on that particular crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you telling us that you never heard of any crimes being committed by Arkan's Men, Seselj's Men, or White Eagles in the Republika Srpska in 1992? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spent the best part of that period of time in Sarajevo, in Vrace, and then later I went to Bijeljina. You've given me all these names, but I wasn't aware of most of them at the time. I knew there were some volunteers in the VRS. Were those Seselj's Men, Carli's Men, Jovic's Men? They were under the jurisdiction of the VRS, and they deployed them in their units the best they could. I don't think they were marked out as something special or different; marked out, in other words, as Seselj's Men, as Jovic's Men, and so on and so forth. There was no way I could have known that they constituted some sort of a special or separate component.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
